newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says Albright origins won't change her views.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says Albright origins won't change her views.

text.p: The Clinton administration said on Tuesday that the discovery that Secretary of State Madeleine Albright appears to be of Jewish ancestry in no way complicated her ability to encourage peace in the Middle East.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters Albright herself briefed President Bill Clinton and Vice President Al Gore on the matter on Monday.
"The president said it was a fascinating story and encouraged Madeleine to find out more, to look into her family history," McCurry said. "He thought it was fascinating."

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said that, based on newly available information, the Czech-born Albright believed it was "more than likely" her grandparents were Jewish and three of them died in the Holocaust.

The Washington Post recently researched Albright's background and reported on Tuesday that more than a dozen of her relatives, including three grandparents, were killed as Jewish victims of the Holocaust in Czechoslovakia.

"Based on the information she has received, Secretary Albright believes it is more than likely that these events occurred," Burns said. But he said Albright, 59, and her family felt a need to follow up on the Post's research and confirm their genealogy themselves.

Burns said Albright had believed from an early age that she was Roman Catholic and only now was coming to understand her heritage was Jewish. She was raised as a Catholic but later became an Episcopalian.
Asked on Tuesday if the discovery might in any way complicate Albright's efforts to encourage the Middle East peace process, McCurry replied: "No."

"There are three great monotheistic traditions that consider the Middle East a holy place and we have talented diplomats from all three religious traditions that work on the Middle East peace process," he added.
At the State Department, Burns told a news briefing the discovery "in no way, shape or form will have any impact whatsoever on her performance or her outlook as secretary of state."

"I think that we can trust that leaders around the world, particularly those in the Middle East, will be sophisticated enough to understand who she is, and who she works for," he said. "I don't anticipate this being an issue whatsoever."

Burns insisted that Albright "didn't know anything about this" until last week when questioned by the Washington Post. He said the Post had given Albright the results of its research and "she intends to follow this up."

He said that since Albright was nominated in December to be secretary of state she had received a great deal of mail from Eastern Europe, some of which referred to the fact that her family might have Jewish roots.

"A lot of this mail referred to stories about her father or her which were clearly inaccurate. And so she didn't pay much attention to it," he said. "Frankly, so much came in at a very busy time that she didn't look."
Albright was 2 when her parents left Czechoslovakia in 1939, less than two weeks after the Nazi occupation. The family eventually came to the United States.
